extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, law students, patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: A doctrinal reference (index/excerpt) listing legal standards and evidentiary rules used to evaluate patentability, enforcement, infringement, procedure before the Patent Office, and equitable remedies. It summarizes legal tests (e.g., identity, novelty, extension, estoppel) and procedural/evidentiary guidance relevant to patent practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estoppel by neglect / permitting rival patent
rubrics_metrics.description: Equitable estoppel arising from a patentee's neglect to sue infringers or permitting a known rival to obtain a patent (e.g., 'by neglect to sue infringers'; 'by permitting known rival to obtain patent'; loss of rights by delay).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts may bar relief where the patentee's inaction misled others (references: 981, 984). Delay in applying for a patent or permitting public use by a rival can defeat priority; interplay with prior inventor and public use doctrines noted.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence — direct and circumstantial; comparative value
rubrics_metrics.description: Both direct and circumstantial evidence are relevant in patent litigation; negative evidence can be important.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comparative value of different classes of evidence is recognized ('direct and circumstantial, comparative value of'; 'negative, important when'). Rules of evidence in the Patent Office are the same as in courts but do not govern uncontested cases. Evidence admissibility varies by forum (law vs equity) and proceeding (e.g., interferences).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence — timing of objections and suppression
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural rules about objections to evidence in equity and law: when objections are too late, suppression motions, and availability of evidence after dismissal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In equity, objections may be waived if raised too late; evidence not properly objected may be unavailable in argument. Motion to suppress and motions taken under bills that were dismissed may still be available for future use (citations: 1116 n.4; 1128; 1160 ii.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office examiners — duties and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Duties of Patent Office examiners, their status as judicial officers since 1861, and limits on their jurisdiction (including deference to Commissioner decisions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must follow Commissioner decisions on law and fact and the rules of courts; they are bound by conclusions of predecessors in some cases. They handle interviews with applicants, both initial examinations and on appeal; examiners of interferences have exclusive jurisdiction over declared interference issues but examiners lack jurisdiction over patentability in some contexts (references: 424; 51 n.4; 558; 573; 504 n.8; 598; 606).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examination of applications in the Patent Office
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedural and substantive examination of patent applications in the Patent Office (see 'Application for Patent').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General reference to examination process and related procedural rules (citation: 53).

rubrics_metrics.name: Excellence or convenience does not show inventive act
rubrics_metrics.description: An increase in excellence or convenience alone does not demonstrate an inventive act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improvements that merely enhance convenience or excellence, without inventive skill, are insufficient to establish patentability (reference: 940 a.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use — definition and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: What constitutes experimental (or experimental/public) use and its effect on prior use/abandonment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experimental use may not be a public use and therefore may not be a bar (e.g., 'not a public use', 'not a public use though use be in public'). Experiments may not constitute abandonment; profit-producing experiments raise issues. See examples and cases (citations: 855 n.8; 955).

rubrics_metrics.name: Experiments are not inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unsuccessful or merely experimental trials are not themselves inventions for patentability purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unsuccessful experiments and mere trials are not inventions; unsuccessful experiments have illustrative instances and proof requirements. Experiments by others do not necessarily negate inventive skill in the succeeding inventor. Experiments are not evidence of prior use (citations: 80 a.1,9; 818 n.8; 84; 199; 318).

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert evidence in patent cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Expert testimony may assist in determining identity and other technical questions in patent litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expert witnesses (scientific and mechanical) are admissible to aid on identity between patented and accused inventions; weight and admissibility depend on circumstances (citations: 892 a.1; 1013-1014; 1041 a.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Extension of letters-patent — standards for grant
rubrics_metrics.description: Criteria and procedure for granting an extension of patent term (extension of letters-patent).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extensions are intended for the inventor's benefit, not assignees; not affected by assignment or re-issue; granted only when inventor has not already received due compensation from the public benefit conferred. Value to the public and lack of due compensation must be shown. Extensions must be confined to the original invention and rest on last re-issue granted with inventor consent; not granted for unimportant parts. Patent Office decisions on these applications are final in many respects; extensions do not shield patent from all defenses in infringement suits and cannot be collaterally attacked for fraud (citations: 835-845; 836-839; 842-844; 837,841).

rubrics_metrics.name: False suggestion in description is fatal
rubrics_metrics.description: A false suggestion in the patent description can be fatal to the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material falsehoods or false suggestions in the specification may render the patent invalid (citation: 494).

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal and state court jurisdiction over patent matters
rubrics_metrics.description: Allocation of jurisdiction between federal and state courts for patent-related claims; scope of federal equity powers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts have jurisdiction over many patent questions and possess ordinary equity powers (citations: 853-866; 1256; 1094). They generally lack jurisdiction over certain license issues in some contexts. See cross-references to circuit/supreme courts and state courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent Office fees and payment consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules about payment of Patent Office fees: how payable, effects of non-payment, and fees for re-issue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fees must be paid as prescribed; no fees for re-issue to correct Office mistakes; non-payment can forfeit an application but does not render an issued patent void; final payment and timing rules apply (citations: 554; 638; 585; 584).

rubrics_metrics.name: File wrapper as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent file-wrapper (prosecution history) and its contents as evidence in litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: File-wrapper contents are admissible as evidence (e.g., on prior use); absence of papers from the file-wrapper is not evidence that such papers do not exist. File-wrapper weight varies by context (citations: 1015; 1019 n.4; 1026 n.18; 1032 n.6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle/force of nature not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'force' or principle of nature employed in an invention is not itself patentable or claimable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural forces/principles cannot be claimed as inventions; change in natural condition or a new mode of controlling a force may be patentable as an application, but the principle itself is not. The concept of 'force' is treated as the essence or mode of an invention in some analyses (citations: 101-102; 135; 98 a.1; 164 a.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign patents and foreign use — effect on U.S. rights
rubrics_metrics.description: How foreign patents, foreign invention dates, and foreign use affect U.S. patent rights and priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A foreign patent is not necessarily a bar to a domestic patent; foreign use is not necessarily equivalent to knowledge in the U.S.; effect depends on issuance to the same patentee and timing. Dates and assignments interplay with U.S. law (citations: 461; 360 a.3; 683; 978 a.4; 1043).

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic/genus vs species rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules governing genus and species inventions: what a genus claim covers and constraints after species patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A genus may be claimed but is not patentable after a species within it has been patented; a patent for a genus covers the species; an inventor of a species may claim the genus in some circumstances but must describe species. Requirements for describing species and examples cited (citations: 471 ll.4,760; 535; 462 n.1; 585).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grant of letters-patent — statutory prerequisites and effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Requirements for a valid grant of letters-patent, its form, and legal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grants are governed by statute and Patent Office rules; illegal unless prerequisites fulfilled; form (signature, record) matters. A grant of 'all patentee's rights' carries an exclusive right and creates implied warranties; certain words (e.g., 'all our right') imply a patent exists. Grants are protected by law and serve as evidence (citations: 422-632; 763; 791-794; 1015).

rubrics_metrics.name: Grantees and assignees — rights and limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiation between grantees and assignees and the rights, obligations, and limits of each.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Grantees and assignees are not synonymous; grantees may be estopped to deny grantor title while enjoying benefits; joint-grantees' rights and obligations (e.g., suing in own names) and territorial restrictions on manufacture/sale are detailed. Transfer, restriction, and vendees' rights discussed (citations: 760 n.2; 794 n.3; 799; 793; 1191 n.8; 1204).

rubrics_metrics.name: Identity — tests for identity between patents and accused devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Identity is a mixed question of fact and law concerning whether accused subject matter is the same as that protected by a patent; identity may be in effect, function, or means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identity is a factual question and may be shown by identity of means, not merely theory; requires consideration of function, mode of operation, and effects. Identity may exist despite differences in shape, size, materials, arrangement, equivalents, or number of parts. Tests differ by type (machines, manufactures, compositions, combinations); expert evidence admissible; presumptions regarding two patented inventions exist (citations: 273; 288; 274; 229; 237; 107; 1026; 892 n.1; 896).

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvement — definition and patentability standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Standards for when an improvement is a distinct, patentable invention versus an unpatentable variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An improvement implies an original and is related to the original; it is distinct if it involves inventive skill. Improvements must be reduced to practice to be patentable; may be analyzed by essential nature, mode of operation, and effects. Improvements cannot claim the original invention and may be restricted by prior patents (citations: 210; 307-318; 219; 220; 218; 307-312; 530-539).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fraud in procurement or sale of patents — consequences and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Treatment of fraud allegations in patent contexts (procurement, sale, concealment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Threat of suit is not fraud; fraud in procuring a patent normally is not available as a collateral attack in some contexts; equity will not relieve one guilty of fraud; the burden of proof lies on the party alleging fraud (citations: 1247 a.2; 967; 715; 717; 1114 a.5; 644 a.1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Function versus means in claim construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinction between claiming a function and claiming means; how courts construe functional claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Function is distinct from means, end, effect; a claim for function may be void in some contexts, but claims for function are often construed to cover corresponding means if possible. The function is the measure of the means; claims for a machine's function are scrutinized (citations: 144; 145; 232; 234; 518; 539 n.1; 530).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — definition and measurement by claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement is the unlawful making, using, or selling of the patented invention, measured by the patent claims (not by the patentee's theory).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement is a mixed question of law and fact and must show identity with the patented invention as claimed. Only what is claimed controls; unclaimed matter is not considered. If a patent is confined to one form, other forms may not infringe. Two patents are presumed not identical. Identity requires identity in means, not merely purpose, function, or effect (citations: 890-894; 891 a.4; 881; 891 a.1; 883).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — acts constituting infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: List of acts that constitute infringement: making, using, selling, offering, supplying parts with intent, and participation in profits of an infringing enterprise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Infringement includes any act promoting unlawful making, use, or sale, including direct participation in profits. Making for experiment or exhibition is not infringement unless beneficially used. Sale of parts with intent that they be united into the patented combination can infringe. Sale abroad, acts before grant, and acts after expiration have special rules. Motive is immaterial; intent may be relevant to damages and willfulness (citations: 897-906; 898; 903-905; 908-909; 918-924).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — actors and vicarious liability
rubrics_metrics.description: Who may commit infringement: individuals, corporate officers, employees, licensees, co-owners, public bodies and limitations on governmental liability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The United States generally is immune (claims against US must be in Court of Claims). Officers, employees, corporations, municipal bodies, contractors, agents, and licensees can incur liability depending on control and benefit. Licensees acting within license scope do not infringe; departures from license may create infringement and contractual remedies. Co-owners and vendees have particular rules (citations: 910-921; 910 n.6; 911-912; 915-917; 913-916; 905; 979; 1044).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement — combination patents, elements, and arts/processes
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules for infringement of combination patents, patents to elements, and patents for processes/arts; what acts constitute infringement for each category.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For combination patents, omission or substitution of material parts typically avoids infringement; use of an unclaimed element or sub-combination is not infringement. Selling an element with intent it be combined may infringe. A patent for an element can be infringed by its use in a combination. For a patent to an art or process, infringement may be continuing and involves use of steps; for machines, manufactures, compositions, and designs there are particular acts that constitute infringement (citations: 922-929; 993; 925 n.2; 926-929).
